transcript.text: Hi, my Hotpoint Aquarius dryer is taking forever to dry and the top gets really hot. Model is TCM580GUK if that helps

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. A dryer that takes ages to dry but gets very hot on top is almost always suffering from restricted airflow. When air can't escape, heat builds up inside, making the casing hot and stopping the clothes from drying efficiently. The most common cause is a blocked lint filter or condenser unit. Before we look at any parts, please check these two things:
1. Is your machine vented (has a hose going out of the back) or a condenser/heat-pump model? This changes how we diagnose it.
2. Clean the lint filter in the door opening and, if you have one, remove the condenser unit from behind the flap at the bottom front. Rinse it under the tap to remove fluff build-up. Was it clogged with fluff before cleaning? Also, were the clothes very wet when they went in (e.g., from a low spin speed on your washer) or was the drum overloaded? A normal load that is well-spun should dry much faster once airflow is clear.

Thank you. It's a condenser model, so there's no hose at the back. The door filter had a thick layer of fluff on it (I'll admit I sometimes forget to clean it), and the condenser at the bottom front had lint packed on the fins, but it looked much cleaner after I rinsed it. It was a normal load from a 1400 spin washer. I should also mention the top panel gets very hot, and I often run the dryer while I'm out at work.

It makes perfect sense why the top was getting so hot: with that much fluff blocking the airflow, the dryer couldn't vent the heat properly, causing the casing to warm up and likely triggering a safety device called a thermal cut-out (TOC) which stops the heater from working to prevent a fire. We need to see if the heater is actually turning on now. The overheating may have tripped that cut-out, meaning no heat is being generated even though the drum is tumbling. 1. Is the drum getting warm or hot inside?
2. Do you feel any airflow coming out of the condenser unit at the bottom front (it should be blowing air out)? If it stays cool, the thermal cut-out has likely tripped and needs resetting or replacing. If it gets hot but still doesn't dry well, we'll look at the fan or internal ducting.

Yes, the drum does heat up and it gets warm inside, so I don't think it has stopped heating. The drum turns normally and water does collect in the container, which was half full and emptied fine. I'm not sure about the airflow at the bottom front, I couldn't really tell either way.

Since the drum is getting warm and water is collecting, the heater is working. However, because the top gets very hot and drying takes forever even after cleaning the main filters, the heat isn't being carried away effectively. This usually means either the fan isn't moving enough air, or there's a blockage in the internal ducting behind the condenser unit that we can't see. Please run a normal cycle for about 10 minutes with the condenser unit removed (keep it safe nearby). Check if you feel strong airflow through that slot. If the air is weak or non-existent, the fan motor is likely failing or blocked. Let me know what you find with the airflow.
I'm happy to try that, but I honestly wouldn't know what counts as strong or weak airflow, so I'm not sure I could judge it. Is there anything else I can check that's easier to tell?

It is difficult to judge airflow strength without a reference point, so let's look for the physical cause of that restriction instead. The air is likely being blocked somewhere deeper inside—either by fluff packed behind the condenser unit or around the fan housing. 1. Look into the slot where the condenser sits at the bottom front. Is there a visible blockage of fluff or debris right behind it?
2. Open the door and spin the drum by hand. Does it turn smoothly, or does it feel stiff, grindy, or make a scraping noise? A hot top can sometimes indicate excessive friction from worn drum rollers. If you find a blockage, clear it carefully with a vacuum or a long brush. If the drum feels rough or noisy, that points to a mechanical fault requiring an engineer. Let me know what you see and feel.

I can't see any obvious fluff or debris in the slot behind the condenser, but I'm not sure how far in I can really see. I didn't notice any scraping or grinding from the drum, only the normal tumbling noise. There's also a faint warm, dusty smell in the room when it runs, though it's not a strong burning smell.

The fact that it still gets very hot and takes forever to dry, even with clean filters, suggests the air is getting trapped inside because it can't move fast enough. This could be a blockage deeper in the internal ducting (which we can't see from the front) or the fan itself isn't pulling hard enough. It's not necessarily a fire risk yet, but it suggests heat is building up where it shouldn't be. Since judging airflow by hand is tricky, let's look inside. We need to remove the top panel to see the fan and ducting clearly. Please switch off and unplug the dryer first. Then, locate the two screws at the very back of the top panel (under the lip) and remove them. Slide the top panel forward about 2cm and lift it up to release the front clips. This will expose the internal components including the fan housing and ducting behind the condenser slot. Please check if there is a dense blockage of fluff in the duct leading from the drum to the condenser, or if the fan blade (visible through the slot) spins freely by hand and looks intact.

Thank you, but I'm not comfortable taking the top panel off, as I don't open up the machine's panels myself. Is there anything else I can check from the outside, or should this be looked at by an engineer?

Since you are not comfortable opening the panels and the external filters have been cleaned but the machine is still taking a long time to dry while getting very hot on top, this points to an internal blockage (likely fluff packed around the fan housing or in the ducting) or a failing blower fan. These components are located inside the casing and cannot be safely accessed without dismantling the unit. While it hasn't reached a strong burning stage yet, running a condenser dryer in this state carries a fire risk because the heat has nowhere to go. I recommend you stop using the machine and arrange for an engineer to inspect it. Continuing to run it risks tripping the thermal cut-out repeatedly or, in a worst-case scenario, causing a fire.
[Safety panel] Overheating can be a fire risk. Clean the lint filter and make sure the airflow/vent isn't blocked, and don't leave the dryer running unattended. If it smells of burning, stop using it and unplug it.

candidates: Restricted airflow (blocked lint filter or condenser) (high)
Faulty heating element or thermal cut-out (if vented/condenser) (low)
